new_statements.rule_in_words: Nouns (and other non-verbs): stress the penultimate syllable unless the final syllable has a coda (l, r, nasal, glide, s), in which case the final syllable is stressed (plánta 'plant', minjér 'woman'); verbs take final stress regardless of syllable weight (plantá 'to plant', kumé 'to eat', bambú). A phonological word formed by the 1sg clitic N plus a verb with a prenasalized initial consonant shifts stress to that initial 'left-heavy' syllable (N ntíndi 'I understood' vs. N pañá 'I caught').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed by Andrade & Kihm. Chapouto 2014 p. 17 reports Bull 1989 p. 77: trisyllabic nouns stressed on the last syllable carry a secondary stress on the first syllable, and numerals of more than three syllables have main stress on the penult with secondary stress on the first syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: A residue of nouns falls outside the rule (lápis 'pencil', penult despite heavy final; sángra 'hen coop'); plural -s does not make the final syllable heavy (kásas vs. kabás); the initial-stress rule for N + prenasalized verb is stated only for disyllabic verbs. Chapouto 2014 (pp. 41-42, fn. 37, fn. 45) found her Bissau informants conforming to the noun rule but not the verb-final rule (they judged verb stress 'generally penultimate'). Almeida 1991 p. 5 notes that suffixed object pronouns shift stress to the last syllable. Couto 1994 (per Chapouto) entertains a tonal contour for traditional creole.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical (word) stress; the authors abstract away from its phonetic realization (intensity/pitch/duration), referring to Kihm & Laks 1989 for that. Domain is the phonological word, which includes the proclitic N 'I' and enclitic object pronouns.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Andrade & Kihm 2000, 'K') describes Guinea-Bissau Kriyol proper, i.e. the Bissau-based standard variety (language-level uppe1455; Glottolog dialect biss1249 Bissau-Bolama Creole). The Casamance/Ziguinchor dialect (cach1242 Cacheu-Ziguinchor Creole) is described separately by Biagui & Quint (APiCS ch. 34) as having lexically distinctive stress on the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable, so the two varieties should not be merged under one stress reading without checking Biagui 2012. Chapouto 2014's Bissau informants also disputed verb-final stress.

sources.note: Kriyol (K) nouns: stress on the penult unless the final syllable is heavy (realized coda l, r, N, glide, s), then final; verbs: final stress irrespective of syllable structure; residue nouns like lápis; plural -s does not make a syllable heavy; after the clitic N 'I' a disyllabic verb with prenasalized onset takes initial stress (N ntíndi), formalised as rule (15) p. 12.

sources.citation: Biagui, Noël Bernard & Nicolas Quint. 2013. Casamancese Creole. APiCS Online survey chapter 34.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Section 4: 'Casamancese Creole is a stress language. Each content word has a stressed syllable.. (1) final: kortá.. (2) penultimate: kárgu.. (3) antepenultimate: lárguma.. Stress has a distinctive function: kónta "(pearl) necklace" vs. kontá "tell"'; open stressed penults are lengthened phonetically. This is the Ziguinchor dialect (Glottolog cach1242).
